comments.author: @BennedicktusPeter
comments.text:
The question about "why build Nusantara when they already have Jakarta? Are they abandoning Jakarta to sink?"

The answer to that is: yes, somewhat. Jakarta is the fastest sinking city in the world, and the burden of administrative center of Indonesia also brings a lot of people, along with their families, to the city that is already bursting at its seams. The original plan was to separate the administrative capital of Indonesia to "safer grounds", where they can have a blank slate to properly design a new, more centralized, capital city for Indonesia. But of course nothing is that simple.

There are a lot of nuances of why Nusantara was built. Some says that it's to mitigate civil unrest, the capital city being inside a forest makes it more manageable to control. Also it being on a literally different island from Java, the world's most populated island, makes it pretty safe from a major civil unrest. 

Others say to mitigate natural disaster from completely annihilating the Indonesian government. This is also true, Kalimantan is more tectonically stable than Java which sits directly on top of the ring of fire, and Nusantara being inside a forest some kilometers away from shore protects it from tsunamis

comments.text:
Flevoland is a new Dutch province, reclaimed from what was once the Zuiderzee; it lies approximately 6 meters below sea level. In terms of total surface area, Flevoland is about 3.2 times the size of Singapore. The province comprises two cities, a nature reserve, and agricultural land. 

The cities of Almere and Lelystad (the provincial capital) were built in the 1980s. Almere has 230,000 inhabitants and is the fastest-growing city in the Netherlands, with a target population of 350,000. The provincial capital, Lelystad, has approximately 85,000 residents. 

The nature reserve, which has only limited public access, provides a habitat for wild horses, bulls, deer, foxes, and even camels. Along the coastlines, atolls have been created for birds migrating between Northern and Southern Europe. 

The rest of Flevoland consists of a patchwork of agricultural land. The soil is highly fertile, and, thanks in part to Flevoland’s large-scale agricultural sector, the Netherlands has become the world’s second-largest exporter of agricultural products, trailing only the United States. 

Flevoland also hosts the highest number of onshore wind turbines in the Netherlands, in fact, more than the rest of the country combined. It was relatively easy to install them there, as there was no opposition from a local population, unlike in other parts of the country.
